utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the response will then deal with the Prosecution's suggestion that we would then have to allow another document as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if I made any mistakes between the first one and the second one, which was first and which one second, I'm clear the one was about three, the other one was about one, and it's only the Prosecution positions in relation to the three that they made this counter proposal. If ... Mr. Tieger, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The order was also correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Order was also correct. Then finally I perhaps spoke even a bit too early because we only received a courtesy copy. It may be that your response has been filed to the second single motion already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, both responses were filed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's on the record as well. Then we'll hear later you from. Mr. Ivetic, having dealt with these practical matters, please address this Chamber with your part of the final argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have the first slide already on the screen. And, Your Honours, before I begin, I would like to point out that we have filed under protest and subject to a reservation of rights a final trial brief which consists of 933 pages where we have performed an in-depth analysis of the many different ways that we believe the Prosecution has failed to meet the burden of proof and in which the law and evidence mandates that conclusion. We will get to burden of proof in a little bit, but first I want to just acknowledge that we will not be repeating nor addressing everything that we have said in our brief, and that should not be misconstrued as a waiver of anything, because often we are just standing on those complete and detailed submissions. I feel I have to be very clear and specific because I heard the Prosecution Monday throwing around words like "admission" for things that don't fit such a legal definition. So I want to be extra careful and clear. And we will get to that admissions issue later too. Now, the Prosecution has taken issue with some of the things we have said in our final brief during their closing arguments, and I might not get to address each and every single one of those things here orally the next few days, and I want to tell you right now that such omission also is not to be construed as a waiver of our argument or admission that the Prosecution is correct. The Prosecution is incorrect in their analysis, and they misconstrue and turn upside down the law on burden of proof. On Monday, the Prosecution was talking about a lot of things that they say we didn't prove in our final brief. The Prosecution says the Defence assertions have not been proven and our Defence falls apart. It should be clear under the law of this Tribunal that it is not our burden. We do not have to prove the things in our final brief. We need only to establish reasonable doubt for General Mladic, and if we have done so as to any material element, you must find him not guilty. We see the Prosecution's attempt to shift the burden of proof upon the Defence and a direct attempt at manipulating and confusing the Court and court staff. The Defence does not have such a burden in these proceedings. We only have a burden as to the alibi in respect of Srebrenica. And respectfully, the Prosecution stipulated to much of our alibi evidence so I submit we met the burden as to that. That stipulation to this proven alibi is clearly reasonable doubt by itself. That alibi is our only burden. For the rest of the case, it is the Prosecution's burden to prove each and every element beyond a reasonable doubt. Why are they talking about our case instead of theirs? That means that they've lost. Their case is that weak. The Prosecution tries impose the burden on the Defence to hide the weaknesses of their own case. The General Mladic Defence team rejects having a burden shifted upon it to prove anything. General Mladic has always told me, "Danny, I want you to seek out the truth," and that is all we are doing. We are helping Your Honours determine the truth by testing and confronting the Prosecution evidence and if they have met the requisite burden. They want you to look through a pinhole at things out of context. We want you to open your eyes and look at the whole of the evidence in a panorama. If we could now go to the second slide. I want to clarify and explain things for those that are mistaken about the Defence having a burden of proof in these proceedings. Maybe there was a misunderstanding of a comment by Your Honour, Judge Orie, during the testimony of Pelemis, where you commented innocent people can come to court to prove their innocence. You might remember that Prosecutor McCloskey jumped up to try and correctly understand what you meant, and that you clarified, Judge Orie, by saying: "No, I think I emphasised that already earlier. But some people who are charged before a court take the position that they'll defend themselves by proving their innocence, whereas it goes without saying that that's not what you have to do. But of course, you are not forbidden to do that. But even if you have not proven your innocence and if the prosecution has not proven your guilt, then you still should be acquitted despite the fact that you have not proven your innocence because that's not required for an acquittal. Is this understood by everyone sufficiently so as to avoid any confusion for the future?" I know that Mr. McCloskey and I were listening that day and we are not confused, but I fear some others in this courtroom, perhaps on his side or perhaps in the public might be confused, and I hope that your explanation clarifies things and leads in Your Honours' review of the Prosecution's submissions. Please, Your Honours, my client, the general, would like to have you stay true your promise to acquit him even if we don't prove his innocence, since the Prosecution fails to meet their burden of proving his guilt. What I will now do is highlight certain things and direct attention to certain questions raised by the evidence and the submissions of the Prosecution which we submit have bearing and relevance to the determination of whether the reasonable doubt standard has been met and, if so, to what parts of the Prosecution case. Now, it is my professional duty, my obligation, to stress to you and to the Prosecution and to the public watching these proceedings, and to my client, what the burden of proof means and how the evidence is to be assessed. I submit that the Prosecution's closing arguments, which have talked of why you should side with their "better" conclusions rather than those obvious exculpatory ones that can be drawn from the evidence, are actually misstating the standard of the burden of proof. As to the better conclusions, we had Mr. Traldi at transcript page 44.366 to -7 talk about a better definition of "liberate." Your Honours, if two alternative and reasonable conclusions exist under the evidence, you are not allowed to take the Prosecution's "better" version, you are compelled to acquit. The second you are forced to speculate, you shall also conclude that there is reasonable doubt. If I can have the next slide. So, please, let us take a look at this and understand this accurate representation of the legal levels of burden of proof. Innocent until proven guilty. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt. These are not just cliches or catch phrases. They are meaningful standards and burdens imposed on the Prosecution to avoid wrongful convictions. Can you think of anything worse than being wrongfully charged and convicted of a crime. Most enlightened legal systems in the world are founded on the basic premise that criminal convictions have such a terrible impact on a person's life and liberty. That is why we require the highest level of proof in order to find a person guilty of a crime. When you are charged with a crime, from the simplest offence all the way up to genocide, the Prosecution must prove your guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The fact that General Mladic has been arrested, confined, or indicted for criminal offences should not give rise to any inference of guilt at this trial. In fact, we should all agree that he sits here innocent before us right now. The fact that the media and international negotiators or Prosecution witnesses have made opinions about Mr. Mladic's guilt should make you even more circumspect and cautious and not sway you as to any inference of guilt. For instance, the Prosecution in closing has recited to you improper legal conclusions of international witnesses on matters of the crimes alleged clearly attempting to invade your legal domain. You must reject the arguments that because a UN official or international negotiator or journalist concluded that Ratko Mladic was in charge or that he was engaging in ethnic cleansing, or any other legal conclusions of criminal responsibility. At transcript pages 44327, 44481, and 44327, the Prosecution made such submissions in their closing. That is not how the Prosecution proves their case. That is not how the burden of proof is satisfied. Your Honours, it is not enough to just say that the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty. The accused is presumed under Article 21(3) to be innocent at all times until proven guilty. General Mladic is innocent. Until you get to the very tip-top of the pyramid, General Mladic is innocent. And again the law says General Mladic is innocent today. You must continue to treat General Mladic as innocent regardless of what the media says, regardless of what the Prosecution argues, because what they and I say today are only arguments, not evidence. What is their story to get around the obvious lack of actual evidence. It is their story. Does it make sense? Or does it leave you questioning. If you are questioning, you must acquit. Even if not questioning their story, that still isn't enough because their story isn't evidence. The Prosecution must establish by the evidence each and every element of the offences beyond a reasonable doubt. That is, to the top tip of the pyramid. And the Trial Chamber must resolve every doubt in favour of the accused with the principle of in dubio pro reo. That is what the Delic Trial Judgement says at paragraph 23. Probable cause which we see on this pyramid is what was required for Mr. Mladic to be arrested, and that's near the bottom of the pyramid. That is where we are today. And that is not enough for a conviction. The Prosecution's evidence must raise the level of certainty first to preponderance, and that is generally explained as proof supporting a story such that it has a "greater than 50 probability" of occurring. And if the evidence takes you there, that may be enough for the public and news media to convict or for civil charges in civil cases, but it is not enough in a criminal case, and you must acquit. And then if the evidence gets you up to the next level, clear and convincing, that still mandates an acquittal because it is not enough. Another way to look at that level is when someone tells you: There are multiple interpretations available but take our version because it is the better definition. And, again, that's exactly what the Prosecution were telling us this past Monday. Your Honours, they are arguing for the wrong standard. Apparently they don't understand that clear and convincing is not enough. Any time that there are other conclusions available under the evidence, it doesn't matter which is better, sounder or more likely, you must acquit. Because only when you get to the very tip-top of the pyramid, when the conclusion of guilt is the sole and only conclusion with no other interpretations in evidence, only then can you convict. Just the tip and only the tip. Any plurality of explanations must mean an acquittal. If they push anything more than just the tip, you have to shake your head and say: No, no, game over, you must acquit. And so why was the Prosecution arguing for a lower standard? Because they're unsure of their evidence? They know they cannot attain the highest level of burden of proof? I know Your Honours were listening. And if you missed it, please go read the transcript where the Prosecution told us essentially that you must acquit General Mladic because they said you have to listen to their better definition. They cannot remove all doubt and get to the top of this pyramid with the evidence they have. So every time in the closing or the final brief when the Prosecution says there is a better interpretation, or they say that something exculpatory General Mladic has written is a lie, that he is covering for some other real intention, that establishes reasonable doubt. During trial, I hope you will recall how many times we would have to call up in re-direct the same document used in Prosecution cross and then direct to the very next line or paragraph which was exactly the opposite or contrary to what the Prosecution had just said the document proved. If the Prosecution is misstating or misrepresenting the evidence, that is an acquittal. So seemingly the Prosecution has made our job easier and Your Honours'. You don't have to deliberate. They conceded on Monday that their case is not up to the top of the pyramid because they argued for you to disregard other conclusions to go with the "better" one. That is reasonable doubt. Under the law, you can deliberate together right now and enter an acquittal just based on what the Prosecution has said. That amounts to an admission. That is an admission on the part of the Prosecution, a real admission, not this fantasy definition that we heard from the Prosecution that went too far and wants to try to sneak up to the top of the pyramid. At transcript page 44.408, when they told us that Pyers Tucker's testimony is not hearsay but rather an admission of Mr. Mladic. If Pyers Tucker heard directly from Mr. Mladic out of court in B/C/S and came to court to tell us what Mladic said, that is the very definition of hearsay. If Pyers Tucker heard from a translator second-hand what Mladic told the translator in B/C/S all out of court and if Tucker came here to testify as to that, then it is a textbook definition of double hearsay. Although admissible, it would still be assessed for its weight and, respectfully, it would be a low weight. The Prosecution is trying to sell you on the notion that this is an admission and not hearsay. The Prosecution dares to take it upon themselves to change the law and definitions under the law to suit what the weaknesses of this case are, all to get a wrongful conviction, by hoping the Court will adopt a lesser degree than reasonable doubt. The case law is very clear. The test when inferring intent from the acts of an accused is that the inference has to be the "only reasonable inference available." The Vasiljevic Appeal Judgement, paragraph 128. All inferences from circumstantial evidence must be the only reasonable conclusion available. That is what you said, Judge Moloto, in the Martic Trial Judgement, paragraph 24. If there is any other reasonable interpretation of the evidence against the accused other than guilt, he must be acquitted. That is what you said, Judge Orie, in the Oric Judgement, paragraph 15, and in the Haradinaj Judgement, paragraph 7. These are not just my words that I am telling you that you have to follow. They are your words. The Prosecution is trying to change your words and your law, your holdings. Don't let them do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I have some problems in attributing to individual Judges a judgement which is delivered by a Chamber, and apart from that, in the Oric judgement, my role there, I don't know what you meant there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did I say -- I meant Haradinaj, Your Honour. I must have misspoke if I said Oric. I meant Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still then, Haradinaj was a Chamber judgement. There was no separate opinion or anything. So, therefore, I take it that you have referred to us as persons as a member of the Bench, that you're referring to the judgement of the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is not necessarily always the same as a personal judgement. I just -- for very formal reasons, I put this on the record. But you are rightly drawing our attention to judgements delivered by Chambers of which we were part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also luckily the right decisions and not the Oric decision. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I was just about to clarify, the one misstatement. Now, if we could go -- if we can actually -- well, I will be skipping the next slide, but we don't need to go to the next one after that. The Prosecution is trying to re-write and change the rules and the law in order to argue for a conviction. We all know it is the most difficult burden to get to the tip of the pyramid. We need to trust that Your Honours value every person's life and liberty so highly that you will make sure that my client is not sent to spend the rest of his days in prison for a crime he may not have committed. That is what is at stake here. The ability of Mr. Mladic to go home, to spend time peacefully with his loved ones around him and then eventually to die at home, surrounded by those that he loves, not to spend the rest of his days in a concrete cage in jail. Society says you have to be absolutely sure that the Prosecution case has nailed the guilt before you send someone to die in prison. We have to treat everyone the same. Ratko Mladic does not get less rights because he is Ratko Mladic. Due process says you must treat Ratko Mladic as you would want to see one of your loved ones, like a member of your family treated if accused of a crime. If you would not want to see a family member convicted based on the little evidence that we have here, then you must acquit Ratko Mladic too. Mr. Tieger and Mr. Traldi made no fewer than 98 references and allegations against President Karadzic in what was supposed to be the first day of the best case they had against General Mladic. And, by the way, the Defence would like to stress that the Prosecution misrepresents what -- misrepresents that our final brief is trying to pass guilt onto Karadzic. In fact, we have taken the position that the Prosecution has not proven any of the JCEs existed at all and that means neither Karadzic, Mladic, nor anyone else is guilty. In our brief, what we have done is to analyse the evidence to demonstrate even if we take the Prosecution's case at its highest, and even if arguendo the allegations against Karadzic or others are valid, there would be no support for naming Mr. Mladic as a member of that putative JCE. Mladic's acts and deeds argue against any involvement in a JCE. That is why the bulk of the Prosecution's JCE allegations centre around statements made by other persons. Why does Mladic have to be guilty by association? General Mladic may have been an island of code and honour amongst despots. He may be to Serbia what General Patton or General McArthur are to the United States. He was a soldier's general. He was a general caught between the proverbial rock and a hard place, tasked with the ultimate catch-22, a truly impossible mission. He did his job to defend his people and country as a soldier should and tried not to get involved in politics. If they already have Karadzic and these other people they named who have been convicted, each of them able to effectuate the crime on their own, why is Mladic necessary? In fact, the very convictions of others provide reasonable doubt, an alternate theory for guilt and plausible deniability for General Mladic. If we can go to the next slide and have that ready. The Prosecution asks you to put on blinders. They would prefer you look at the world through a peephole. We heard Mr. Tieger talking about Srebrenica, and he talked about two things that he said proved Mladic guilty. One of them is this TV interview that we now have on the screen. It's P1147 and it was discussed at transcript page 44.329. Where General Mladic still is going through Srebrenica to Potocari. He still does not know what he will find at Potocari. He is still expecting to find an enemy force waiting for him to do battle with. Is that the "revenge" he is talking about? Engaging in a battle mano a mano, hand to hand, against an armed combatant to finally and soundly defeat them? This is a replay of a long-standing conflict where Naser Oric's Muslim forces in Srebrenica had displaced the indigenous Serbian people from the area by deadly raids on neighbouring Serb villages which resulted in deaths of 1300 Serbs. Militarily defeating Oric's forces and allowing the return of Serbs to their homes in the greater Srebrenica area would be a fitting and honourable form of revenge. The evidence supports it, and it is a reasonable inference, and, thus, it creates reasonable doubt. Another interpretation is available. Maybe General Mladic meant that the news of Srebrenica's quick defeat would be the shock that would shake the spirit of the armija BiH in the rest of Bosnia and allow everyone to get the complete cessation of hostilities to end the war and the suffering, something which General Mladic had been trying to do in the previous period, while the armija BiH was resisting and avoiding such a cessation of hostilities and instead promoted continued war and bloodshed. We have in evidence, for instance, P2190, P345, P190, and transcript page 16801 for this. That too is a legitimate form of "revenge" and according to common sense is logical and available from the evidence. That, too, is an acquittal. Maybe, just maybe, General Mladic is thinking about how he will treat the civilians with kindness and dignity and thus take the moral high ground over Naser Oric and show Serbs to be dignified, and thus make the enemy forces irate and lose the support of the people and media ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is also an admirable type of revenge. Such revenge could swing the public perception of the ABiH's own actions. This is a further example of reasonable doubt existing under the evidence. The other recorded words of Mr. Mladic are consistent with this in the manner that he spoke to civilians at Potocari, and we will get to that next week. Most importantly, Your Honours, according to the Prosecution final trial brief, at paragraph 1105, the JCE that they allege to murder Srebrenica males did not even exist at this point in time when Mr. Mladic made these words. Now if we could go to the next slide. And now let's talk about the words of Mr. Mladic at the third Fontana meeting. The other day, Mr. Tieger on Monday showed us but he only showed 30 seconds to prove involvement of Mr. Mladic in the horrendous accusations that they were making. Why did the Prosecution not want us to look at more than 30 seconds? Why take Mr. Mladic's words out of context? Because their case is that weak and impotent where the evidence needs to be overwhelming. What about that third Fontana meeting? Let's bring that bad boy back out here and take a look at the entire context of what was said. And I would now ask for the slide to be clicked to play the video. We're not getting sound. Is the sound back on?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at this same Fontana meeting, we see Krstic sitting next to Mladic, and we heard from the Prosecution about the decision. Mr. McCloskey mentioned the two of them having dinner after the meeting "in quiet, comfortable surroundings of a hotel," and called it "decision-making time." That was transcript page 44.552. Mr. McCloskey failed to bring out that the very same General Krstic, the very next day, issued an order, and that's D290 in evidence, and at page 4 that order says: "The civilian Muslim population and UNPROFOR are not targets of our operations. Collect them together and keep them under guard, but crush and destroy armed Muslim groups." And by the way, the dinner in "quiet, comfortable surroundings of a hotel" was made up for the first time in closing. It is not referenced in their final brief nor in the evidence, but we'll deal with that when I make Srebrenica submissions next week. Now let's take into proper context these words uttered by General Mladic at the Fontana meeting and the two other meetings that were prior. Again, at this point in time, General Mladic still does not know where is the opposing military force, Naser Oric's 28th Division. It is uncontroverted in the evidence that Oric's forces were stronger in terms of number of soldiers than the forces that Mladic had at Srebrenica and that they posed a serious risk. We have, for instance, D1448, D270, transcript page 33467, transcript page 10908 to -10. As confirmed by the Dutch soldiers whose evidence we heard, the ABiH is hiding behind civilians as they often have the entire war in a defended city concept. We will expand on defended city later. What this all means is that under this scenario, this Hotel Fontana meeting can be regarded as legitimate military threats against an enemy force instead of the nefarious and twisted interpretation that Mr. Tieger has placed on it and which Mr. McCloskey later was forced to support in closing. If we can go to the next slide. Now, you don't have to accept my word as to a more benign interpretation of that meeting. Let's look to what Prosecution military expert Richard Butler said. Butler watched recordings of all the Fontana meetings, and he told you from a military standpoint there was nothing improper and that these were legitimate albeit harsh words, since Mladic believes that Oric's forces remain in Srebrenica, the 28th Division. And Butler told us both Krivaja 95 and any attacks against the column of 28th Division soldiers in Srebrenica is fair game, legitimate combat. There you have the citations to Mr. Butler's evidence. And, in fact, Prosecutor McCloskey told you that the Krivaja operation is legitimate, and I'm sure you will recall he multiple times said the attacks against the column of the 28th Division is legitimate, just like his expert Butler. Now, you must ask yourself: Are Mladic's comments at the Fontana meeting capable of being understood as benign and logical under the context of a legitimate ongoing military operation against a legitimate military objective, like the continuation of Krivaja 95 or combat against the column of the 28th Division? You bet. That's what the Prosecution's evidence says. So what is Mr. Tieger doing? And why is Mr. McCloskey, the other day, joining Mr. Tieger to disavow their own Prosecution military expert? What is the counter expert or military basis that they use to tell Your Honours that the 30 seconds they showed indicates a criminal intent? The Prosecution is trying to change their evidence because they realise the evidence they brought argues for acquittal. If the Fontana speech is all you have, game over. Draft the acquittal. This is reasonable doubt. At Fontana, General Mladic was trying to save needless loss of life, his soldiers' lives, the lives of any soldiers and the lives of civilians that may be caught in the middle because the ABiH is using them as human shields. And these are only words, not deeds. How dare the Prosecution say otherwise given the standard and burden of proof. Again, why can't General Mladic be a General Patton, a peacemaker, the good guy? Is it because he's a Serb? If the evidence allows more than one interpretation, you are forced by law to vote for the acquittal of General Mladic. Already on the first day of their closing, we were confronted with some problems and some uncertainty, departures from the promises made by the Prosecution in their opening statement and indictment. Because the opening statements and indictment are promises that the Prosecution made to this panel of Judges and also to the public that they are supposed to serve the interests of and a promise to the Defence of what their case was going to be, what they were going to prove, by the evidence and according to the appropriate standard. The case they are arguing now is not what they started out with and there have been significant departures. Before we address the evidence and the Defence arguments as to the counts, I would like to go through some of the relevant legal standards these problems and uncertainties raised by the Prosecution present. And, Your Honours, it is important to look at what the Prosecution promised and what they ended up presenting because it demonstrates two things. First, it demonstrates that the case they brought is not as strong as the case they promised. This implicates the questions of burden of proof that we have been talking about here today already. Secondly, it relates to the candor of the Prosecution in phrasing and framing the evidence and its presentation to you. If they have to tweak the evidence and contort it to meet the burden, it really isn't good evidence. Now, I don't know why they do it and I don't have the time to go through everything that was promised during the opening statements, but I will raise two stark examples that should lead to the conclusion that those promises should all be compared with what they actually led in evidence. On Tuesday of this week, the Prosecution talked about the use of snipers in Sarajevo as part of their allegations against General Mladic. Let me now remind you what was said during the opening statements by Prosecutor Dermot Groome on the same topic and this is a promise he made to you. If we could please have the next slide. "Mr. Groome: Your Honour, I'm now going to talk about sniping. "Sniping played a different role in the campaign of terror against Sarajevans. The noisy imprecision of the modified air bombs was in contrast to the lethal silence of the sniper's bullet. Sarajevans would hide behind buildings and shipping containers, gathering the courage to dash across a street where others had felled before. "In silent perches around the city, VRS soldiers waited in vantage points above the tram line, above paths civilians had to travel to get food, water, fuel for heat, waiting silently, finger poised on the trigger until someone dared to rush in front of the cross-hairs of a scope. "The main street running along the Miljacka river became so famous for the number of shootings that it was called Sniper's Alley." And then he made his promise, and Mr. Groome said: "One of these snipers will appear before you and provide evidence of this aspect of the campaign of terror. He will describe his orders to shoot at anything that moved down below his perch. Other witnesses will provide evidence of how snipers were trained and how the activity of snipers around the city was co-ordinated." Well, when the trial started, we found out the promised witness wasn't really a sniper. He was an ordinary VRS soldier and he was protecting a building. The witness is protected Witness RM141 so I won't give too many details, but Your Honours will recall that in a filing of June 2012, the Prosecution sought to change the 65 ter summary to say he was not a sniper but worked closely with snipers in another capacity. Then that witness testified, and the story came out that he was tasked with guarding a military location near the front lines and was told to shoot at anything that came across that front line at him. What? The difference could not be more dramatic. The story went from an inculpatory and damning insider witness against General Mladic to a completely benign witness and I dare say a standard description of orders that every soldier in every country would be tasked with, shooting at anything that came across you at the front line. I must stress no witnesses were brought by the Prosecution to fit the promises made by Mr. Groome. Now this is where I have a problem. RM141 had testified previously in no fewer than two prior proceedings, both of them before the Prosecution's opening statements. So I ask you to ask them where did this misleading information come from, since they surely knew this person was not a sniper given that they had presented him in the other trials. More troubling. We have now heard that the Prosecution is sticking to their pre-trial story about sniping in Sarajevo even though their main witness and their testimony fizzled and disappeared. They didn't ask you to remember that part of the evidence. They also did not remind that you General Rose of UNPROFOR wrote that the Muslim police in Bosnia had a special sniping unit meant to shoot at its own civilians in such a way as to implicate the Serb side. That proofing note of General Rose was discussed in evidence with Witnesses Thomas and Fraser. They likewise do not remind you of the Witness Edin Garaplija, himself a member of the Bosnian secret police, who, through his investigations, confirmed that this unit called Seve existed and that it staged many of the sniping incidents in Sarajevo, including the infamous Romeo and Juliet shooting at the bridge. That was at transcript 33916. They also did not remind you that Witness Sergii Moroz told us of other UN personnel reporting to him that Bosnian snipers, Bosnian army snipers would cross over the Miljacka river into the neutral zone between them and Serb territory to fire at Sarajevo from those positions. That was at transcript page 42358 to -59. Is this really their best case? Have they acted in compliance with the duty of candor? And let's consider that with their original plan destroyed when the sniper turned into fairy dust, the Prosecution and Mr. Weber on Wednesday saw no problem in continuing the fiction of what he called snipers ordered to shoot at anything that moves, this time referencing the 2nd Romanija Brigade and two documents, P7809, P7810. This was at transcript page 45.509 to -10. Unfortunately for Mr. Weber, again the persons instructed to shoot at anything that moves are not snipers. They're ordinary soldiers. And again the instruction is issued at a place near the front lines where it is perfectly legitimate. Military expert Kovac has presented the military law on the topic and we will go more into detail on this when talking of Sarajevo next week. But the tenacious efforts of the Prosecution to continually manipulate the evidence to prejudice Your Honours with misleading assertions of proof, that's reasonable doubt. Another representation and promise from the opening, if we can have the next slide. Prosecutor McCloskey promised to you at transcript 508 as follows: "In the fall of 1995, Mladic and Karadzic decided to exhume the enormous mass graves near Orahovac, Petkovci, Kozluk, Branjevo, and Kravica and scatter the human remains into well over 30 smaller graves hidden in isolated areas where they hoped they could not be found by NATO or the ICTY. General Mladic himself approved the enormous amounts of fuel necessary for this task. "In a document signed by General Mladic he stated ..." And then it goes on to describe the fuel. Now, the document in question referred to by Mr. McCloskey is P1500. And at trial, with expert Butler and another witness, the same story was repeated, and Mr. McCloskey stressed that the fuel order was by Mladic in his own hand. That's at transcript page 11.660 to 11.661, and 16.438 to 16.439. Now we have discussed in our final brief at paragraphs 3293 to 3304 this particular document and situation and demonstrate that this document, P1500, in fact, did not have to come from General Mladic. And you can imagine my surprise when I open the Prosecution's final brief to find out that the Prosecution agrees with me and concedes that documents that start with the designation prefix identical to P1500 which is "03/04," it's circled in red on the screen, didn't come from Mladic but came from the operation and training administration. But this is not what they say in their Srebrenica section. Rather, it's at the front end of the brief, several hundred pages removed, at paragraph 54 where they concede this. Your Honours, this concession, admission by the Prosecution admits the Defence arguments that P1500 did not have to emanate from Mladic. And yet at paragraph 1384 of their final brief the Prosecution still insists that this designation, 03/04, comes directly from Mladic. Can they do that? Can they really tell you for this order that their Witness Butler said is potentially the only order that could be deemed to be implicating Mladic in Srebrenica crimes, can they tell that you the only conclusion is the one that he signed it of his own hand and sent it? Can they do that after they have conceded that documents with the 03/04 designation did not come from Mladic's office in the Main Staff? How do they exclude the possibility that someone else, legitimately or illegally, used Mladic's name for their own purposes under this set of facts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't have the ear set, but we can break now. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, before I proceed, I'd like to correct a misstatement that I made when I said RM141 at temporary transcript page 54. I meant to say RM147. And that was brought to my attention by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I couldn't find it, Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, at transcript page 44326, we heard Mr. Tieger start the Prosecution closing talking about the year 1993. But then you heard him say that Ratko Mladic joined the JCE in May of 1992. Then the Prosecution's position changed yet again around transcript page 44389, when they started talking about 1991 which predates the date that Ratko Mladic is alleged to have joined the JCE. And we heard at transcript page 44373 that the Prosecution would like to hold Ratko Mladic accountable for crimes in Croatia in 1991 and crimes in Bosnia in 1991. That was at transcript page 44389 and the next page. After all this time, Your Honours, my client, Ratko Mladic, still does not have a fair and adequate notice from this Prosecution of what exactly is their case against him and what time-period and alleged events it covers. I ask Your Honours, and the public out there: Is this fair? This past week Mr. Tieger spoke about Rule 73 bis (D) and the Defence arguments as to the indictment. In doing so, he confused two separate issues. One is the unfairness in incidents that were removed from the indictment by the crossing off of them by the Prosecution under Rule 73 bis (D). The other category are those things that were never properly written into the indictment in the first place. The Prosecution also confuses the concept of preliminary motions to fix the indictment and the situation we are at now where we are saying that no conviction can stand when the evidence presented is not in line with the indictment as specified. The law of this Tribunal states that the accused cannot be expected to engage in guess-work in order to ascertain what the case is against him, nor can the accused be expected to prepare alternative or entirely new lines of Defence because the Prosecution has failed to make its case clear. The Simic Appeals Judgement, paragraph 71. Further, the Prosecution is expected to know its case before it goes to trial and cannot omit material aspects of its main allegations in the indictment with the aim of molding the case against the accused in the course of trial, depending on the evidence. Both the Djordjevic Appeal Judgement at paragraph 573 and the Simic Appeal Judgement at paragraph 71 talk about this. Now, let's focus on what Mr. Tieger told us Monday. He told us that the crossed-off parts of the indictment are out and that the parts that are empty and were never written in the indictment are still in. That was transcript page 44384. But under such logic, then a blank sheet of paper would suffice as a proper indictment, and that surely is not in accord with the jurisprudence. But more importantly, given what Mr. Tieger said, then why are these crossed-out, dropped incidents of the indictment back in the Prosecution's final brief? On Monday, Mr. Tieger spoke of Croatia and 1991 and again suggested Mr. Mladic's involvement in crimes in Croatia. None of that is in the indictment. We complained to you at the pre-trial conference about this, at transcript page 326 to 327, and asked you to prevent this. Your Honours denied that request by saying that only the indictment can charge the accused and no material changes could be made in other ways but that temporal events beyond the scope may be necessary for terms of context. And then we had the Prosecution case, and at the close of the Prosecution case we found out that rather than context, they actually wanted to use 1991 Croatia crimes for substance in the case. And we again complained to Your Honours, at transcript page 20316-20320, and Your Honours opined as to the extent for which outside temporal events can be used for context. But now the Prosecution wants criminal responsibility for the same. To date, we have not had any type of protection from the Rules of this Tribunal as to notice and pleading requirements to know what this Croatia evidence is. Can Mr. Mladic be convicted on it? Then why wasn't it plead in the indictment? Similarly, RM518 is being used as a Rule 92 quater witness whom the Prosecution is now presenting not only for 1991 and Croatia, but for purposes of attempting to prove wholesale parts of the alleged overarching JCE. This evidence from a 92 quater witness admitted in written form only, and if uncorroborated, according to the law, it cannot be used as a basis for conviction. Look, for instance, at the Milutinovic Trial Judgement, volume 3, paragraph 243 for this type of ruling. And yet in the Prosecution's final trial brief RM518's evidence is cited 17 times. Five citations are completely uncorroborated. That's at citations, the footnotes, 765, 769, 771, 773, and 794 of the Prosecution's brief. And two citations do not support the Prosecution's averments in the final brief. That's at 9 and 963, footnotes. Neither the pre-trial brief nor the 65 ter summary indicated fully the manner of how RM518's evidence was going to be presented to prove material elements. Some of the averments in the final brief of the Prosecution relate to direct acts and conducts alleged of the accused via this uncorroborated 92 quater witness. Is that enough for a conviction? No, Your Honours. Now even more strangely, we heard from Mr. Traldi at transcript page 44399 that even unscheduled incidents can corroborate the evidence. And so under this logic, I suppose, even the crossed-out portions as well as unscheduled incidents can be relied upon according to the Prosecution. The Prosecution position on Rule 73 bis (D) is contrary to ICTY jurisprudence on the issue. Other ICTY cases have clearly held that the Prosecution is not permitted to lead evidence on parts of the indictment that are excluded under Rule 73 bis (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just for the record, did you say on page 61, line 4, that "even scheduled incidents can corroborate" or did you say "unscheduled incidents"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I meant to say "unscheduled," but to be honest, if -- I may have said "scheduled." So thank you for catching that. I meant to say "unscheduled incidents."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Under the jurisprudence, unless the -- strike that. Let me start at the beginning of the line. Other ICTY cases have clearly held that the Prosecution is not permitted to lead evidence on parts of the indictment that are excluded against Rule -- are excluded under Rule 73 bis (D) unless the Prosecution applies for such evidence to be heard and included under Rule 73 bis (F) and obtains a court decision permitting same. That was not done here. In the Milutinovic et al Trial Chamber, after submissions of the parties, pursuant to Rule 73 bis (D), to limit the Prosecution indictment, the charges in relation to Racak, Padaliste and Dubrava prison were removed. Thereafter in that case, the Prosecution attempted to lead evidence which related to Racak and Padaliste, and at trial the Chamber intervened and prevented such back-door attempts to get around the Rule 73 bis (D) decision. And in this case, we are having the Prosecution to try to revive counts, incidents, that were crossed out. Now, according to the Tribunal Statute, General Mladic is to be treated equally with others that have been before him at the ICTY, and thus we submit that his rights should not be curtailed or diluted in relation to the ability of the Prosecution to proceed with either unindicted, unscheduled matters that are not in the indictment or matters that were in the indictment but were removed from the same by the application of Rule 73 bis (D). And focussing on how the Prosecution applied 73 bis (D) to our case, when it moved for reduction in the charges under the rule, the Prosecution promised that if it sought to later lead and rely on evidence from the dropped charges for mens rea, it would give specific notice in the Rule 65 ter summaries before leading the same. It failed to do so, and now is relying upon evidence in the final trial brief for no fewer than two of the dropped detention facilities in Sokolac; C18.1 and C18.2. Four dropped detention facilities in Kotor Varos; C11.1, C11.2, C11.3, C11.4. And five dropped detention facilities in Sanski Most; C17.1, C17.2, C17.3, C17.4, and C17.5. That's, in total, 11 previously dropped detention facilities. But Mr. Tieger told us everything that is crossed off in the indictment is out. So which is it? The Prosecution wants to have everything that is missing from the indictment, everything that was crossed out and dropped, and everything else. How is Mr. Mladic supposed to know what to defend against in such a scenario? This is not a hypothetical or academic exercise because I will now tell you that at the Prosecution's final brief at paragraph 1225 there are eight completely new charges for destructions of mosques for whom criminal liability is claimed as to Srebrenica. These are nowhere to be found in the indictment. How badly does the Prosecution think it is doing? Do they think they are losing that they now decide to throw a surprise claim of mosque destruction to beef up their case? In the indictment, paragraph 59 states that the destruction of cultural sites is limited to Schedule D. Not a single mosque from Srebrenica is in Schedule D. Where is the notice? Do we now get to seek a reopening of the trial to try to defend these new charges? Is it fair if we don't get that chance? Will the Prosecution try to raise new charges during next week's rebuttal, or perhaps at the judgement? There has to be a line drawn. It is supposed to be drawn in the indictment. That isn't all. When we look at annex B of the indictment as to other mosques and compare it to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, we find that the number of affected religious sites do not match up between the two, in regards to Kljuc, Kotor Varos, Sanski Most, Vlasenica, and Ilidza. Why are the numbers different? For which ones now do we have to defend? This is an untenable situation. Your Honours can correct all of this in the judgement by preventing this Prosecution attempt and dismissing those charges. In our final brief at pages 6 to 9, we talk about other charges for which there is absolutely nothing written in the schedules about alleged crime sites. How can we be held in suspense until the very end of the case to know what it was that we were supposed to defend against? There are entire counts for which they have no notice in the indictment. This practice renders the notice provisions and protections of the Tribunal totally meaningless. You have already heard from Mr. Lukic about how incredibly vague and nebulous and over-expansive the indictment was as to JCE. Your Honours may recall some discussion at the beginning of the case that the Prosecution could not provide more details. Perhaps if you have -- if you have read the Prosecution's final brief, you were perhaps shocked, like we were, to find in the final brief that they now know precise names and positions of persons whom they allege are members -- direct members of the JCE who are not pleaded with particularity in the indictment. Look at Srebrenica, for example, paragraphs 1066, 1081, 1086. There are likely, I think a dozen or so names that are never specified in the indictment and are for the first time formally identified as JCE members in the final brief. Is that fair? Some of these persons were Prosecution witnesses who denied any part of the JCE. How is the Defence to have fair notice to do its job? On Monday, during one of the breaks in the proceedings, my client asked me, "Danny, will President Karadzic be coming here later to defend himself against Tieger or do we have to defend President Karadzic in our closing too?" Indeed, Your Honours, I understand and appreciate that Mr. Tieger was on the Karadzic case longer than he was on the Mladic case and that he may be stuck in that mindset, but I'm also conscious of another possibility; namely that the Prosecution is trying to play on the emotions and institutional knowledge of your staff members, your helpers, who came over from the Karadzic case after drafting that judgement which convicted Mr. Karadzic and which in its text tried to convict Mr. Mladic and are now drafting the judgement already as we speak in this case. Clearly the Prosecution are trying to manipulate things in that way. Now we have mentioned a few times duty of candor. Since it is called by different names in different jurisdictions, I want to spend some time on that to make sure we all understand what I am talking about. Under United States law, candor is a duty that has long existed for prosecutor's which is best explained by the 1935 case of Berger v. US. If I can have the next slide. And in that case, you see the holdings that are up on the screen, and the key there is that the interests of the prosecutor is not that it shall win a case but that justice shall be done, and that they should refrain from improper methods calculated to produce a wrongful conviction. Now, under US law, the duty of candor has been applied to raise and punish serious questions of prosecutorial misconduct, including for taking two inconsistent positions in two separate criminal proceedings against two accused. Smith v. Groose, 205 F.3d 1045 (8th Circuit 2000) is one such example. Such a duty extends to informing the court correctly about the law and facts of a case so that the court may arrive at correct conclusions and render exact justice. Per the US Supreme Court in Brady v. Maryland, 373 US 83 (1963): "Society wins not only when the guilty are convicted, but when criminal trials are fair; our system of the administration of justice suffers when any accused is treated unfairly." Respectfully, the duty of candor does not allow the Prosecution to stay quiet about and thus conceal material facts and law that may assist the Chamber in not being misled. We have not performed an exhaustive review of the world's legal systems, but can report that we have found such a duty exists under various names within the United Nations, Canada, Britain, Australia, South Africa, Kenya, and Ireland. If we can have the next slide, please. Here, we see from the guide-lines on the role of prosecutors adopted by the 8th United Nations Congress on the prevention of crime and the treatment of offenders from 1990, again, language similar to what we looked at before. If I can have the next slide. And, again, from the Canadian jurisprudence in Rex v. Chamandy, 61 C.C.C. 224 from 1934, that, again, a criminal prosecution is not a contest between individuals. It is an investigation conducted without feelings or animus on the part of the prosecution with a single view of determining the truth. Your Honours, I submit that some of the Prosecution's tactics and things that have happened in these proceedings need to be viewed through the lens of the existing duty of candor. Including what I have already spoken about, I would highlight the following. In regards to Prijedor, which we will discuss later, there is an issue in that the Prosecution is presenting faulty evidence and incompatible theories in this case which is different from other convictions and cases it has pursued. In those other cases, the perpetrators were civilian MUP and now are being recast as VRS. We will explore that further when I get to Prijedor. But for now, I will mention that in paragraph 33 of the Prosecution's final brief, it is presented that Mr. Mladic is involved in the running of the camps Omarska and Keraterm and that Mr. Mladic was responsible for cleaning up the camps before a Red Cross visit. However, in evidence we have P2432, which is testimony under seal of a protected Prosecution witness, where in that exhibit, the Prosecution - in fact, Mr. Tieger - is presenting that witness and is presenting the evidence that Zupljanin, rather than Mladic, was the one that ordered these facilities cleaned up before the ICRC came and that Drljaca of the civilian MUP ran both centres. Is their case that bad that they must recast history and take diametrically opposed positions to try and get convictions of two persons for the same deed? But let's get back to Srebrenica. Let's recall that the Prosecution started in the opening talking about 7.000 dead at Srebrenica. At trial, the demographers kept creeping that number upwards. But let's recall that the Prosecution demographers did not initially reveal that 70 per cent of their purported victims for the Srebrenica incidents were ABiH soldiers. Defence expert Radovanovic at transcript page 38170 explained that. Let's recall there are resolved issues about some of the victims exhumed from the Srebrenica mass graves who are recorded as having been killed as members of the ABiH in the years prior to 1995; D344 in evidence. And we talk in our final brief at paragraph 2262 to 2263 of the failure of the OTP to account for their own body of evidence from survivors of the Srebrenica column and from their own expert Richard Butler to talk about massive combat casualties of the column. And can you find that at our Defence brief paragraph 2264 and transcript page 16289 to 16290. So where are these dead, these combat casualties? And are they included in the figure being promoted by the Prosecution? And now if we could briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at paragraph 1581 of the Prosecution's final brief, the Prosecution has now reduced the figure of victims for Srebrenica to 5.956. Yet, the other day in closing, Mr. McCloskey again promoted it to "over 7.000" victims. Keep in mind the Prosecution and their demographer have refused to provide the Defence with the matching criteria and insight into how their demographer made the matches to identify all these victims as being related to crimes in Srebrenica. This is a case that the Prosecution must win and get a conviction in. That's their position. It's a case where General Mladic is vilified in the media. It is a case where President Meron of the MICT has assured victims publicly that Mr. Mladic will be brought to justice, and one where President Agius of the Tribunal has already convicted Mr. Mladic of crimes in the Popovic Judgement, absent Mr. Mladic being able to defend himself. The political pressure to convict is great, but duties must not be broken. Duties and the law must be applied evenly and impartially without regard for pressure of political or other nature. Now let's talk about Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you look at the screen, you are kindly requested to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I apologise I should be looking at the screen. Let's talk about Kalinovik, General Mladic's home town. This Prosecution filed a motion seeking for you to take judicial notice of an adjudicated fact, I believe it was from the Galic case, that four named mosques in Kalinovik were destroyed by Bosnian Serb forces. That's adjudicated fact 746. At the same time that they obtained your decision granting that request, the Prosecution surely already had in their possession a report from expert Riedlmayer from the Karadzic case telling them that per his review, the fourth mosque never existed and thus never was destroyed. They do nothing. They bring a witness for Kalinovik, RM034, asking very little of him except for the leading question: "Who destroyed all four mosques in Kalinovik?" And the witness confirms by saying all four mosques were destroyed by Bosnian Serb forces. The Prosecution again keeps quiet. Then Riedlmayer comes and they choose not to ask him about Kalinovik and the mosque that doesn't exist. They keep quiet again. In Rule 98 bis I raise it and point out that the mosque doesn't exist. At that point in time to today, they take no steps to acknowledge this or to seek to drop that charge for that mosque that doesn't exist. Is that how the duty of candor is supposed to work? Respectfully, Your Honours, for these reasons alone, any result other than an acquittal will be marred with a black stain of the Prosecution's mishandling and disrepute which then would forever mar the reputation and legacy of this Tribunal. And since your names and your reputations will be affixed to this judgement, do not let the Prosecution's foul behaviour stain and blemish your reputations. Now I will move to Count 1, the charge of genocide in municipalities. In its final brief, the Prosecution has focused its allegations of genocide solely on an analysis of the events which transpired in Prijedor. Again, on the other day, this week, they pushed Prijedor as the main example for their genocide case in relation to the municipalities. In doing so, they imply that they cannot substantiate a charge of genocide in the municipalities otherwise indicated in their indictment. Similarly, an analysis of this single municipality of Prijedor strongly undermines their assertion that a pattern of crimes existed across the six identified municipalities which, according to the Prosecution, evidences genocide. The other day we listened to the Prosecution say that the Chamber may find that Count 1 has been proven in the aggregate by taking parts from the best evidence from the various municipalities and then using that with Prijedor to draw conclusions of a pattern. No. That surely is not the standard. Cherry-picking the evidence is not the standard for genocide. If there is evidence contrary to genocide, then that is reasonable doubt. If a particular municipality charge is sought to be proven as genocide, it is up to the Prosecution to prove that charge, not to aggregate a lot of bad evidence to link it by association with good evidence. The reason the Prosecution wants you to do this is because it has led very little evidence on most municipalities. There is a lot that is open and unknown. Your Honours, that's reasonable doubt. That is not the top tip of the pyramid. That's somewhere lower. That is an acquittal. The specific intent or the so-called dolus specialis is what genocide distinguishes from other criminal prohibitions. This is an aggravated form of intent and requires not only intent for acts but also intent to commit the acts for purposes of destroying, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such. The intent must be to destroy the group as a separate and distinct entity and target individuals because of their membership of a group. This specific intent cannot be established in this case. When reviewing actions and statements in their proper contexts, it shows there was no intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats that Mr. Mladic had in his mind. Your Honours, in his position as Main Staff commander, General Mladic could have issued orders to commit horrendous crimes. But that is not what General Mladic did. On the contrary. He always insisted that the VRS abide by the Geneva Conventions and customs and laws of war. And most importantly, Mladic issued orders to protect the civilian population. We have multiple witnesses and documents that talk about that. But, for example, on 23 June 1992, the accused ordered the Rogatica Brigade to take measures to protect the Muslim population in the villages of Burati and Vrhbarje [phoen] from possible violence from individuals. That is D1514, page 1 to 2. Is this evidence of an intent to destroy Bosnian Muslims and Croats? No. Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution claims that intent can be inferred from statements made by Mr. Mladic, and in making this claim, they would have you understand these statements out of their context and disregard any and all statements that evidence the contrary. They cannot do this. They have to take the statements together and review them in their context with all the evidence combined. The Karadzic Trial Judgement paragraph 550 says that. And we saw an example today where the full context of the third Fontana meeting is quite different from what was presented by the Prosecution. Now, for example, the Prosecution has misinterpreted Mladic's intent so much, to such an extent as to impose language not used by him in order to prove dolus specialis. For example, contrary to what is alleged in paragraph 381 of their final brief, Mladic did not depict all Bosnian Muslims or Croats as enemies, let alone as historical enemies of the Serb people. Quite the opposite. In P00431, page 33, Mr. Mladic said: "We don't want a war against the Muslims as people or against Croats as people but against those who steered and pitted these peoples against us." The Prosecution has similarly failed to contextualise the statement by Mr. Mladic that all actions were justified in the face of the threat of genocide. This at 381 of the Prosecution's final brief. And the report, the document in which this statement was made, was drafted in the midst of a conflict initiated by the SDA against the SDS and Bosnian Serb people in order to force them to accept SDA political dominance. In that context, Mr. Mladic praised the Bosnian Serb people for their resistance against the believed threat of subjugation and progress towards establishing a democratic community in which people of all ethnicities would be equally respected. P1966, page 3. Furthermore, the Prosecution has attempted to compile unrelated exhibits which have no association in an effort to substantiate dolus specialis in paragraph 381 of their final brief. When viewed in their proper context, none of the referenced exhibits of evidence show any intent to "vanish" or "disappear" any person based upon their ethnicity, let alone an intent to destroy Bosnian Muslims peoples in whole or part. Rather, references are made only to legitimate combat personnel who posed a threat as enemy combatant forces. For example, P1969, referenced by the Prosecution in footnote 1550 of their brief at paragraph 381, Mladic states only that the Ustashas should disappear; and in P3076, Mladic is concerned only to have the enemy vanish, that enemy being the combat forces against which he is defending his people. Moreover, in making these compilations, the Prosecution has also relied upon several documents which do not pertain to the six municipalities referenced in the indictment for genocide. For instance, P327 and P1960. The Prosecution claims that genocidal intent can be evidenced from the satisfaction that Mladic is alleged to have expressed of the actions of fighters in Prijedor in an interview of October 1992. That is paragraph 381 of the Prosecution's brief. It should be noted that he does not reference the VRS. He states only "their fighters." That's P7629, page 2 to 3. And what the Prosecution fails to bring up, in that same interview Mladic also reiterates his commitment to peace, saying, and now I quote Mr. Mladic: "I would like peace to come already during this interview or immediately afterwards, but in my opinion, the problems will not be solved that fast. With regard to the army, we are ready to sit down and talk about peace right now. If the opposing sides demonstrate such will as well, peace would be possible and would be restored quickly." P7629, page 3. This reiterates statements made by General Mladic throughout 1992, including the intercept referenced by the Prosecution P327, page 2 to 3, in which Mladic says: "We are not in favour of fighting. We are in favour of peace." As such, it cannot be concluded that he knew of crimes or that he approved of them from this evidence as much more benign interpretations are available from the plain meaning of the words he used. A high standard must be met to evidence the intent to destroy. Indeed, it has been held that even statements which could indicate an ethnic bias or an intention to separate people based upon ethnicity, those mere words alone are insufficient to demonstrate an intent to physically destroy. At our own Tribunal we can look at the Stakic Trial Judgement, paragraph 519; the Karadzic Trial Judgement, paragraph 2597; and at the ICJ, the judgement in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, paragraph 190. Similarly, the Prosecution would have us believe that any deaths, crimes, injuries or other acts which occurred in the municipalities evidence genocidal intent. They have failed, however, not only to demonstrate Mladic's culpability for such deaths, crimes, injuries or other acts, but also that the acts themselves evidence genocide. In fact, it has been demonstrated that no group was in and of itself deliberately targeted by the VRS. Evidence demonstrating that numerous civilians of all ethnicities were protected by the VRS, despite the incidents which occurred, that defeats the allegation of dolus specialis. That shows that there was no intent to destroy the group in whole or in part in Mr. Mladic's mind. For example, in Rogatica and Kotor Varos, several Muslim villages enjoyed full protection during the conflict. While the Prosecution in their submissions would like to focus on Satorovici, I would again return to the villages of Burati and Vrhpolje, and in evidence is D1514, an order from the Main Staff and signed by General Mladic to the Rogatica Brigade commander. This order was issued after another document, D958, a report on how peaceful and loyal Bosnian Muslim villagers were being harassed by unknown persons. If I can have the next slide. Here we have it in both languages. In this order General Mladic says: "Immediately take a measures to protect the Muslim population in these villages from possible violence from individuals because they expressed loyalty to the Republika Srpska. "2, explain to soldiers and units who will perform the possible effects nearby these villages or those who intercede terror, that any violence against the people of these villages will be politically harmful for Republika Srpska, its army and the Serbian people in general. "3, for execution of this order, unit commanders are personally responsible to me." The evidence is that these villages stayed peacefully with their Serbian neighbours until late into the war and left peacefully due to no reasons related to General Mladic or any JCE. The Prosecution would have you believe that General Mladic has a discriminatory intent to destroy Muslims already in 1992 and yet that's exactly when he is issuing this type of order. General Mladic is acting to protect Bosnian Muslims, including from errant and wrongful acts of fellow Serbs. Your Honours, that's reasonable doubt. That is an acquittal. And in Sanski Most, there were neighbourhoods with more than 1.000 Muslim and Croat inhabitants. That's D785, paragraph 19, as one example of that evidence. The Prosecution took issue with this as well. And I would like to focus on another two of General Mladic's documents. They are D929 and D1503, and they're issued in September and October of 1995 and are addressed to President Karadzic and the MUP police minister, and they relate to Sanski Most. These two documents prove two things: One, they prove that even in that late of a date in 1995 in the war, non-Serbs still reside in the very town of Sanski Most in significant number; two, they show that General Mladic is standing up to try and protect those non-Serbs who were loyal citizens who happened to be Bosnian Muslim and Croat, protect them from crimes and harassment by Arkan. As these documents demonstrate, General Mladic is neither approving of the harassment and crimes being committed by Arkan against non-Serbs, nor is he approving of Arkan and his group. He calls them paramilitaries and suggests that if the police and Karadzic do not act to remove this group, the army will act militarily against Arkan. One cannot turn a blind eye to affirmative evidence of General Ratko Mladic's actions to try and protect non-Serbs, even from his -- from his fellow Serbs. Such actions of Ratko Mladic do not evidence a genocidal criminal intent. Rather, they suggest an interpretation consistent with reasonable doubt, of an honourable soldier trying to save lives and protect all the people of his country, even non-Serbs, in a very difficult and perilous war. Your Honours, that is enough for an acquittal. The Prosecution is nowhere near the top of the pyramid with such evidence. Further, again, I don't know how much detail I will be able to go into next week on the municipalities, but one has to look at the manner in which General Mladic's VRS forces were engaged in the very municipalities where the Prosecution alleges genocide. If we can have the next slide, please. I will look at Kljuc right now. Exhibit P3923 is excerpted on our screens right now, and it was presented by the Prosecution at trial and was submitted to try and show that VRS forces were in villages and areas that were scheduled indictment incidents. It was used with Witness Kevac. The Prosecution's only concern was to demonstrate that the VRS was present. For them, this was enough. Because by the Prosecution's view, the VRS is a criminal entity. Again, for them being a Serb is a criminal offence too. Therefore, the Prosecution chose not to focus on what the VRS actually was ordered to do and what it actually did. The Prosecution ignores the presence of armed enemy combatants of the ABiH side or their activities which necessitated military clearing operations, or ciscenje. So as to a wide area in Kljuc on 30 May 1992, which is this entry in this log-book, mopping up, or ciscenje, was performed to address Bosnian Muslim forces who were armed and active. And now let's look at the results of that action. Results. Arrested, 250 people who surrendered their weapons. After investigation, 100 were released to go home. That doesn't sound like genocide. Next entry. About 1.000 refugees in the village of Ljusa were allowed to return home after a search of nearby villages. Again, that doesn't sound like genocide. Witness Kevac testified that this is consistent with the way the JNA and VRS conducted mopping up, or ciscenje, operations. That's at transcript page 30541 to 30544. Again, Your Honours, this evidence does not support a finding of any discriminatory intent or any genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock. We're close to the moment where we have to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could just perhaps have 20 seconds to finish this paragraph, it will be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 seconds you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This supports a finding of legitimate military actions aimed only against the armed enemy combatants. Why else would some people with guns be allowed to go home? Because they are found not to have used their weapons, not to have posed a threat. And if a temporary removal of the civilian population during mopping up or combat is followed by a return of these civilians to their homes, well, there's only one result that can be reached under this under law, that is an acquittal. And I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Before we adjourn, I would have one or two small questions for you. Only a few minutes ago you referred to D929 and D1503 and you say these are documents -- General Mladic's documents issued in September and October of 1995. I can follow that for D1503, but D929 seems to me to be a witness statement rather than a document issued in September, a Mladic document. Further, could I ask you in transcript page 67 today, you refer to your final briefs paragraph 2262, 2263, and 2264, and you did so after you said we would now turn to Srebrenica. 2264 deals with modified air bombs, which are really a Sarajevo issue. And 2262 and 2263 seem to give comment in the context of the evidence given by Mr. Van der Weijden which also places us very much in the Sarajevo area rather than in Srebrenica. And I'm not blaming you for the speed of speech, but, of course, I can't check everything at this moment, but these are just a few sources where I had difficulties to follow you, not in your speech, but in the underlying documents you refer to. We adjourn for the day, but perhaps -- may I take it that the response earlier announced will be in writing and you will -- then we'd like to -- then we'll look at that later today. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume on Monday, the 12th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of December, 2016, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
